title: Null safety you can actually use
summary: Use nullable reference types and guard clauses to make 'no value' explicit instead of accidental.

workedExample.title: Make an unsafe lookup safe
steps: The parameter is `string?`, so the compiler knows `text` may be null. `text.Length` produces a warning and can throw at run time.
Return a nullable result (`int?`) when absence has meaning, or define a deterministic fallback such as `0`. Do not silently pretend a missing string was empty unless that is truly the domain rule.
Option A, explicit absence: `static int? LengthOf(string? text) => text?.Length;`
Option B, fallback with a documented rule: `static int LengthOf(string? text) => text?.Length ?? 0;`
Option C, caller bug: `static int LengthOf(string text) { ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(text); return text.Length; }` — the signature now promises non-null.
Whichever you choose, the type signature tells the truth. That is the core skill: make the possibility of null visible in the type, not hidden in a comment.

bugFix.title: The missing null check
bugFix.explanation: `name` may be null, so `name.Trim()` can throw before the length check ever runs. Guard first, then trim once: `if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name)) return "(anonymous)"; return name.Trim();`. The nullable annotation was correct; the code ignored it.

explainPrompt: Explain the difference between a nullable reference type warning and a runtime null check. Why is `!` dangerous if used casually?

checkQuestions.prompt: What does `string?` mean in a nullable-enabled project?
options: The string is stored on the heap instead of the stack
The reference may be null and callers should handle that
The compiler inserts runtime null checks
checkQuestions.explanation: `string?` is an annotation: the value may be absent. It does not change the runtime representation or insert checks.
optionExplanations: All strings are reference types and live on the heap regardless of annotation.
Mutability is unrelated; strings are immutable.
No runtime checks are inserted by nullable reference types.

checkQuestions.prompt: Which expression provides a safe fallback when `name` may be null?
checkQuestions.explanation: The null-coalescing operator returns the right operand when the left is null.
optionExplanations: This dereferences null and can throw.
The null-forgiving operator only silences warnings.
`string` has no `.Value`; that belongs to nullable value types.

checkQuestions.prompt: When is the null-forgiving operator `!` appropriate?
options: Whenever the compiler warns, to keep the build clean
When you have a real invariant the compiler cannot see, and you accept responsibility
checkQuestions.explanation: `!` is an assertion. It is reasonable when you can justify the invariant, and dangerous when used to silence a genuine bug.
optionExplanations: Silencing warnings without evidence hides bugs.
Correct: it is an assertion of non-nullness.
It applies to nullable reference and value types.
It does not provide a fallback value.
